title: Apricot Jam
subtitle: Bright, tangy apricot preserve for toast and pastry glazing
excerpt: Apricot jam has a sharp, honeyed flavour and sets firmly because the fruit is naturally high in pectin. It doubles as a glazing jam for tarts and pastries. Makes about three 450 g jars.
sourceNotes: Mrs Beeton (PG #10136); Pam Corbin, Preserves. Apricot jam is a double-purpose preserve: table jam and the classic glaze for tarts and croissants.

recipe.freezeNotes: Halved, stoned apricots freeze well for winter jam-making.

glossaryTerms.definition: A thin, warm coat of apricot jam (or other preserve) brushed over pastry or fruit tarts to seal and shine the surface.

content.text: Apricot jam has a clear, honey-orange colour and a sharp-sweet flavour that works as a table jam and as the
for tarts, croissants, and Danish pastries. The skins dissolve during cooking and the fruit's natural pectin gives a firm set without much fuss. Makes about three 450 g jars.
Put the apricots, water, and lemon juice in the pan over medium heat. Simmer, stirring gently, until the fruit is completely soft and beginning to collapse, about 10 minutes.
Add sugar and boil to setting point

Add the sugar and stir over low heat until dissolved. Raise to a full rolling boil and cook for 10 to 15 minutes. Test on a cold plate from 10 minutes. When the surface wrinkles, take off the heat, skim, rest 5 minutes, then ladle into hot sterilised jars and seal.

items.cause: Fruit was not simmered long enough before the sugar went in.
items.fix: Simmer until the skins are fully softened before adding sugar. Once sugar is in, skins stop softening.

items.cause: Commercial apricots are often less acidic than home-grown.
items.fix: Add an extra tablespoon of lemon juice to balance.

items.cause: Prolonged boiling caramelises the fruit sugars.
items.fix: Use the widest pan available to speed evaporation and reach setting point quickly.

items.cause: Very ripe apricots are lower in pectin.
items.fix: Add the juice of 1 lemon and boil for another 5 minutes. Alternatively, add 1 tsp pectin dissolved in a tablespoon of lemon juice.

content.text: Using apricot jam as a glaze

Warm 3 to 4 tbsp of jam in a small saucepan with a splash of water until liquid and smooth. Push through a sieve if you want a completely clear glaze, then brush over tarts or pastries while still warm. It sets as it cools.
